# Add a `--json` flag to `faff eligible`

## WHY
`faff eligible` prints a bare `true`/`false` on stdout. Callers that want the resolved precedence (which label won, what the default was) have to re-derive it. A structured mode lets tooling read the reasoning without parsing prose.

## WHAT
Add an opt-in `--json` flag. Default output is unchanged (bare `true`/`false`). With `--json`, print a one-line object `{ "eligible": bool, "basis": "hold|automate|default", "default": "opt-in|opt-out" }` to stdout and nothing else.

## HOW
**Chosen:** thread a `json` boolean through the existing `cmdEligible` handler. The verdict + basis are already computed by the shared `resolveEligibility` helper; `--json` only changes the *rendering* of that result, never the resolution. Bare mode stays byte-identical.

## Scenarios
1. `faff eligible --label faff-automate --json` → `{ "eligible": true, "basis": "automate", "default": "opt-in" }`, exit 0.
2. `faff eligible --label faff-automation-hold --label faff-automate --json` → `{ "eligible": false, "basis": "hold", "default": "opt-in" }` (hold wins).
3. `faff eligible --label faff-automate` (no `--json`) → bare `true` (unchanged).

## DONE
- [ ] `--json` emits the object shape above; bare mode is byte-identical to today.
- [ ] `basis` reflects the winning precedence tier (hold > automate > default).
- [ ] a unit test covers all three scenarios.
